brief.head: No cluster by decree
brief.text: Clusters mat­ter, Ajay Shah said, but they emerge or­gan­i­cally, as in Tirupur’s gar­ments and Gujarat’s chem­i­cals. “It is not true that you can will these into ex­is­tence.” {089-C03}

brief.head: Lobby, don’t compete
brief.text: Decades of a pro­tected econ­omy[[x4]] taught Indian firms to get ahead by work­ing the state, Amit Varma said: too often an Indian en­tre­pre­neur asks how to in­flu­ence a joint sec­re­tary[[x3]]. {089-C12}

brief.head: Method over machine
brief.text: To an en­gi­neer a tech­nol­ogy is a ma­chine, Ajay Shah said; to an econ­o­mist it is tech­nique[[x5]]. Productivity lives in know-how, learned by doing. {089-C15}

brief.head: Growth is the defence
brief.text: The army should solve the prob­lem of Chinese back­doors for it­self, Ajay Shah said, not turn the whole econ­omy against for­eign­ers. Strength comes from 8 per cent growth. {089-C18}

brief.head: Unhappy in its own way
brief.text: China’s EVs and solar pan­els are cherry-picked suc­cesses, Ajay Shah said. In the round, “all suc­cess­ful ad­vanced economies look alike. All un­happy, poor coun­tries are un­happy in their own way.” {089-C19}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.who: Ajay Shah, on why many private long shots beat one government champion[[x6]]

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on states that pick winners
lead.head: Don’t pick winners, enable them

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 89

play.label: Hear the case, step by step

body: A fan wrote to Amit Varma to say that he and Ajay Shah were so smart they should plan India’s econ­omy. Varma found those last lines deeply dis­turb­ing. {089-S01}

You can plan your own day, he replied, but not a coun­try. “Planning a coun­try is just a con­cep­tion of great hubris,” Varma said. “Our hero Friedrich Hayek called it the fatal con­ceit[[x1]].” {089-C01}
Industrial pol­icy, he said, is a clas­sic case of that top-down think­ing, and should not be done bet­ter. It should not be done at all.

Shah had learnt hu­mil­ity the hard way. As a “cal­low” 35-year-old hired into the Ministry of Finance by Yashwant Sinha, he found within days that the job was truly hard, and that “there are no ob­vi­ous mis­takes”. {089-S02}
## Four ways to pick a win­ner
Industrial pol­icy, Shah said, is “the game of a gov­ern­ment that picks win­ners”: this in­dus­try, tech­nol­ogy, firm or place of pro­duc­tion is good, that one bad. {089-C02}

The state has four levers for it: sub­si­dies, co­er­cive power, ethno-nationalism and out­right mo­nop­oly. With the first, Varma ob­served, it plays ven­ture cap­i­tal­ist; with the last, en­tre­pre­neur.
Shah’s premise was arith­metic. GDP is the sum of the value added by firms, so “the story of eco­nomic de­vel­op­ment is cen­trally a story of firms”, and of the in­cen­tives they face. {089-C04}
Subsidies, he ar­gued, put the state in place of fi­nance. Finance places many long shots, most of which fail; a gov­ern­ment backs one cham­pion through thick and thin. {089-C06}

Public money is dearer still. People and firms re­or­gan­ise their lives to dodge tax, and pay lawyers and ac­coun­tants be­sides. “It turns out that the mar­ginal cost of pub­lic funds is three,” Shah said. {#mcpf}
Varma went fur­ther: every in­ter­ven­tion in free mar­kets, he said, “amounts to a re­dis­tri­bu­tion of wealth from the poor to the rich”. {089-C08}
## Patches and pro­tec­tion

The government’s pro­duc­tion-linked in­cen­tives, or PLI, com­pen­sate firms such as Apple for mis­takes in India’s in­di­rect taxes. Shah agreed that Apple de­served it, but wanted the tax sys­tem fixed at the root, so that thou­sands of other global firms would come too. {089-C13}

Protection fails twice over, Varma ar­gued. A tar­iff on a bet­ter for­eign rival hurts con­sumers, and spares the Indian firm the need to im­prove. “You’re hurt­ing the con­sumer and you’re hurt­ing the Indian com­pany.” {089-C17}

The fourth lever is the bluntest. Air India began as a Tata com­pany, was taken over by the gov­ern­ment and made a mo­nop­oly, turned into a zom­bie firm liv­ing on pub­lic money, and was fi­nally sold back to the Tatas.
## The state’s real job

The job of pol­icy, Shah said, “is to en­able win­ners, not pick win­ners”: fund re­search in an in­dus­try-neutral way, keep com­pe­ti­tion fierce from start-up to bank­ruptcy, open the econ­omy to trade and for­eign firms, and wel­come im­mi­grants. {089-C20}
Varma added a cau­tion: most mo­nop­o­lies exist only with the state’s col­lu­sion, so its job is chiefly the rule of law.

Shah closed with SEEPZ, a walled zone set up in north Bombay in the 1970s so that ra­dios could be made for ex­port. The in­dus­tries that flour­ished there were two that no plan­ner fore­saw: di­a­mond pol­ish­ing and com­puter soft­ware.
“You can’t pre­dict, you can’t con­trol,” Shah said, “but adding free­dom is al­ways a good thing.” {089-S08}

second.label: Capital controls
second.head: Chickens get the credit
second.deck: The RBI once let nine industries borrow abroad. Ajay Shah read the list

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the RBI’s chosen industries

body: The Reserve Bank of India has long po­liced bor­row­ing from abroad, and Ajay Shah has never seen an eco­nomic rea­son for it. One day a rule said ex­ter­nal com­mer­cial bor­row­ing would be al­lowed for nine in­dus­tries only. {#nine}

Those cho­sen would get cheaper for­eign credit; the rest would not. Shah, “bloody minded and masochis­tic” enough to read such doc­u­ments, found that the list in­cluded nan­otech­nol­ogy and poul­try farms. “Amit, you’re not eat­ing enough chicken,” he said. {089-S04}
Amit Varma fore­saw “re­ally tiny chick­ens”. Ask at a poul­try farm for the sub­sidised bird, he said, and you will be told: “we have nano chick­ens.” {089-J04}

quote.text: Chicken needs cheap credit. So we will give ex­clu­sive ac­cess to ex­ter­nal com­mer­cial bor­row­ing to poul­try farms.

third.head: Indians export, not India

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the export target

body: Ajay Shah was the ju­nior-most per­son in the room at a Ministry of Finance meet­ing run by Ashok Lahiri, then chief eco­nomic ad­vi­sor. On the rou­tine agenda: the Ministry of Commerce set­ting a tar­get for India’s ex­ports[[x2]]. {089-S03}
Shah asked what the Ministry of Commerce, or any of them, had to do with what India ex­ports. “India is a col­lec­tion of peo­ple, and those peo­ple ex­port,” he said.

Exporting de­ci­sions are made by in­di­vid­ual firms, he ar­gued. The state can cre­ate en­abling con­di­tions; what ex­ports ac­tu­ally ma­te­ri­alise hap­pens in so­ci­ety, and is not for a gov­ern­ment to plan, con­trol or set a tar­get for.
Even the word tar­get, Shah said, is “semi-offensive”: miss it, and an ur­gent mid-year meet­ing is called to think up “pol­icy mea­sures to boost ex­ports”. {#target}

p2.title: The four levers
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s anatomy of industrial policy, lever by lever, and what the state should do instead {089-C02}

quote.text: Indians are not in­fe­rior. Sundar Pichai is an Indian. Satya Nadella is an Indian. So there’s noth­ing wrong with Indians.

photo.caption: Friedrich Hayek, economist, in a portrait released by the Mises Institute

box.title: The conceit behind the plan
box.text: Friedrich Hayek’s *The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism*[[x7]][[x8]] names the error at the heart of the episode. A na­tion, Amit Varma said, is too com­plex for any­one to plan from the top, how­ever en­light­ened the plan­ner. {089-R01}

sections.label: The idea
sections.head: A ministry for every trade
sections.caption: what industrial policy is
body: Industrial pol­icy, Ajay Shah said, is the game of a gov­ern­ment that picks win­ners. Officials de­cide which in­dus­try, tech­nol­ogy, firm or place of pro­duc­tion is good and which is bad. When such de­ci­sions are placed in the hands of the gov­ern­ment, “it’s called in­dus­trial pol­icy”. {089-C02}
Growing up in India, he said, you see the whole fir­ma­ment: min­istries of in­dus­try, tex­tiles, chem­i­cals, steel and IT, and spe­cial at­ten­tion for hand­looms.
## Grown, not de­clared

Clusters show where the line is crossed. Silicon Valley, Tirupur’s gar­ments and Gujarat’s chem­i­cals grew or­gan­i­cally, as skills, ven­dors and labour mar­kets gath­ered. Governments see them and try to de­clare their own, Shah said, and the choice gets con­tam­i­nated by “eq­uity”, every state want­ing one, or by a pow­er­ful politician’s con­stituency. {089-C03}

Behind this lies his cen­tral claim. GDP is the sum of the value added by firms, and rich coun­tries are full of high-productivity firms. People are the same ev­ery­where: Sundar Pichai and Satya Nadella are Indians. What dif­fers is the in­cen­tives of the op­er­at­ing en­vi­ron­ment. {089-C04}

~ Amit Varma put it his own way: growth hap­pens through firms, as en­trepreneurs scram­ble to ful­fil each other’s needs, and the government’s job is to pro­vide a rule of law under which they com­pete with­out co­er­cion.

quote.text: Indians are not in­fe­rior. Sundar Pichai is an Indian. Satya Nadella is an Indian. So there’s noth­ing wrong with Indians.

sections.label: Lever one
sections.head: The rupee that costs three
sections.caption: subsidies and public money
body: A sub­sidy can be a tax break, a cheap input or cash, Ajay Shah said, but it al­ways boils down to pub­lic money. His first ques­tion was why a gov­ern­ment should do what fi­nance al­ready does: if poul­try farms are a great in­vest­ment, buy their shares or lend to them.

If Indian fi­nance works poorly, he said, the fix is to re­pair it and let for­eign fi­nan­cial firms in. Finance hunts all day for the next good op­por­tu­nity, plac­ing dozens of long shots, most of which fail, while a gov­ern­ment backs one na­tional cham­pion through thick and thin. {089-C06}
Shah reached for Oliver Cromwell: “in the bow­els of Christ, con­sider it pos­si­ble you may be mis­taken.” {089-J17}
## Blood money

Public money, he said, is “co­erced out of the peo­ple”. People re­or­gan­ise their lives to avoid tax, and the econ­omy car­ries lawyers, ac­counts de­part­ments and jails. Each rupee spent costs about three[[x9]] in GDP, which de­fence or a vac­ci­na­tion cam­paign can jus­tify, and poul­try farms can­not. {089-C07}

~ Amit Varma added Milton Friedman’s ma­trix. Spend your own money on your­self and you both economise and seek value. The gov­ern­ment spends some­body else’s money on some­body else, and does nei­ther. {089-C09}

quote.text: Public money is co­erced out of the peo­ple. Taxation has blood on it.

sections.label: The folly of PLI
sections.head: Paying back what tax took
sections.caption: production-linked incentives
body: Production-linked in­cen­tives, or PLI, are the government’s new ef­fort at pay­ing sub­si­dies ex­plic­itly to some in­dus­tries. Export sub­si­dies break WTO rules, Ajay Shah ex­plained, so the pay­ments are tied to pro­duc­tion.
Shah called Apple’s pres­ence in India a great achieve­ment, one that could push local ven­dors from hun­dred-micron er­rors to one-micron ones.
## Small er­rors, big swings

Ila Patnaik, he said, taught him how much small tax mis­takes mat­ter. The profit after tax of the av­er­age non-financial Indian firm is 6 per cent of sales, so an in­di­rect-tax error of 1 to 3 per cent can swing its re­turn on eq­uity hugely. {#pat}
Good coun­tries re­fund in­di­rect taxes to ex­porters[[x10]], be­cause you do not tax for­eign­ers. India does not, so Apple is right to ask for com­pen­sa­tion, and PLI pro­vides it. {089-C13}

But only gi­ants can af­ford what Shah de­scribed as a $10 mil­lion op­er­a­tion in Delhi, to ne­go­ti­ate with gov­ern­ment and ac­tu­ally get paid. {#tenmn} Fix the tax sys­tem at the root[[x11]], he said, and thou­sands of global firms would do more in India.

~ Other “dis­abil­i­ties”, such as costly trans­port, er­ratic elec­tric­ity or un­skilled work­ers, de­serve not a shred of at­ten­tion, he added. With some of the world’s low­est wages, firms in India have “a huge sort of neg­a­tive dis­abil­ity” in their pocket. {089-C14}

quote.text: PLI is a re­ver­sal of in­ap­pro­pri­ate tax­a­tion. A sim­ple dharma of pub­lic fi­nance is you don’t tax non-residents.

sections.label: Lever two
sections.head: A camera doesn’t make Nomsita
sections.caption: coercion and technology
body: Coercion is the lever Amit Varma hates most, and Ajay Shah ex­plained why it spreads. Spending is reined in by a bud­get that has to add up. “There’s no bud­get con­straint of co­er­cive power[[x12]],” he said. {089-C05}

When the state backs one tech­nol­ogy, as with in­come tax in­spec­tors who can fine shops that refuse UPI, it as­sumes it knows best. Nobody in gov­ern­ment can sur­vey the world’s com­plex­ity and choose, Shah said. Multiple rival stan­dards bat­tling for supremacy are a healthy thing.
## Machines and know-how
Those who push a tech­nol­ogy think pro­duc­tiv­ity lives in the ma­chine. To an en­gi­neer, Shah said, tech­nol­ogy is a ma­chine; to an econ­o­mist, it is ev­ery­thing about tech­nique. {089-C15}
Give an army great tanks and it does not be­come world class. And if any idiot had a Sony Alpha cam­era, he said, “they do not be­come Nomsita”[[x13]], who shoots the show. {089-J06}
Know-how is learned by doing, and it trav­els through peo­ple, such as alumni of Hindustan Lever who car­ried Unilever’s knowl­edge into new con­sumer goods com­pa­nies.
~ Varma added that tech­nol­ogy never stands still, and that you have to be at the cut­ting edge of the ecosys­tem to re­ally un­der­stand it.

quote.text: To an en­gi­neer, a tech­nol­ogy is a ma­chine. To an econ­o­mist, tech­nol­ogy is ev­ery­thing about tech­nique.

sections.label: Lever three
sections.head: The firm that never grows up
sections.caption: protection and foreign firms
body: The third lever, ethno-nationalism, favours Indian firms and keeps for­eign­ers out. Ajay Shah could not imag­ine the uni­verse in which it works. How will you ever make Indian firms bet­ter, he asked, by re­duc­ing the com­pet­i­tive pres­sure on them[[x15]] from global firms?
The state of the art lives in­side for­eign firms, so their pres­ence spreads know-how across India. “If any­thing you want it up­side down,” he said. “You want more for­eign firms here.” {089-C16}
Even “Indian firm” is slip­pery: ICICI Bank is 90 per cent owned by for­eign­ers, and Microsoft has an Indian CEO. {#icici}
## Seen and un­seen

Amit Varma set out protectionism’s two un­seen ef­fects[[x14]]. When a tar­iff shields Indian firm A from a bet­ter Italian firm X, the seen ef­fect is that A pros­pers. Unseen, con­sumers lose lower prices or bet­ter value, and A, spared the world’s best, stays stuck in a low equi­lib­rium. {089-C17}

National se­cu­rity is a real ex­cep­tion, Shah said: the army should keep Chinese back­doors out of its gear through trusted sup­ply chains and part­ners. That is no rea­son to dis­tort the whole econ­omy. {089-C18}
~ Russia, he noted, has an Italy-sized GDP, which is why Europe can ab­sorb the threat. {089-J09} Varma said many Italian view­ers were at this point deeply dis­ap­pointed.

quote.text: So you’re not even help­ing the Indian com­pany. You’re hurt­ing the con­sumer and you’re hurt­ing the Indian com­pany.

sections.label: The alternative
sections.head: Make life hard for firms
sections.caption: what the state should do
body: Asked what he would do if he did run the coun­try, Ajay Shah of­fered a phrase: the job of pol­icy is “to en­able win­ners, not pick win­ners”. Geniuses are hid­ing in the pri­vate sec­tor, and no­body knows who or where they are. {089-C20}

First comes re­search, con­tracted out to uni­ver­si­ties and pri­vate firms[[x17]] in an in­dus­try-neutral way. He would chal­lenge firms to land a craft on Venus, “a non­sen­si­cal ob­jec­tive” whose spillovers no­body can pre­dict, and fund work on dou­bling the size of an egg. “We want Wright’s law of eggs[[x16]].” {089-J11}
## From start-up to bank­ruptcy
Next comes fierce com­pe­ti­tion. “Life for the firm should never be easy,” he said. Firms must be free to fail and peo­ple to land on their feet: bank­ruptcy is a healthy, nor­mal part of life.

Then deep in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion, with more im­ports and ex­ports, Indian multi­na­tion­als and global firms op­er­at­ing with­out re­stric­tion. And im­mi­gra­tion, so Indian firms can hire from all over the world.
~ Amit Varma added a cau­tion. Nearly every mo­nop­oly, he said, comes about with the col­lu­sion of the state, so the government’s job, as far as pos­si­ble, is a rule of law. {#collusion}

quote.text: The job of gov­ern­ment is to cre­ate con­di­tions where win­ning hap­pens, where some great firms emerge with re­ally high pro­duc­tiv­i­ties.

What the gov­ern­ment does is that it spends some­body else’s money on some­body else. And there­fore the in­cen­tives drive you to­wards nei­ther econ­o­miz­ing nor to­wards seek­ing value. It is the worst way to spend money.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Of walled zones, waiting lists, a lost airline and a fined shopkeeper

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a walled zone in north Bombay
stories.head: Plan radios, get diamonds
body: In the 1970s, some bu­reau­crats looked at East Asia, which was mak­ing ra­dios and elec­tronic parts and ex­port­ing them all over the world, and asked why India could not do the same. Ajay Shah told what hap­pened next as one of the great­est in­dus­trial-policy suc­cesses of world his­tory.
Their di­ag­no­sis was cus­toms duty. Import the tran­sis­tors, pay 150 per cent duty, and a radio made in India would be far too ex­pen­sive to re-export. {#duty}

So in the boon­docks of north Bombay, they built a bound­ary wall around a chunk of land: the Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone[[x18]], or SEEPZ. Every truck com­ing in and out was in­spected.

Components came from the air­port along spe­cial path­ways, prob­a­bly, Shah imag­ined, with some­body rid­ing shot­gun so that no tran­sis­tor was smug­gled into the Indian mar­ket. The fin­ished ra­dios went back to the planes in ar­moured trucks.
Then Indian firms saw what they had been given: free­dom to im­port and to ex­port. Through what Shah called “the or­ganic process of dis­cov­ery and not de­sign”, two great in­dus­tries emerged.

Entrepreneurs brought rough di­a­monds from South Africa and Antwerp, hired cheap Indian labour to pol­ish them and sent them out again. India today pol­ishes about 55 per cent of the world’s di­a­monds by num­ber. {#diamonds}
~ Others im­ported com­put­ers, so that Indian pro­gram­mers could build soft­ware for ex­port. SEEPZ be­came one of the early sites of the Indian soft­ware in­dus­try.
stories.why: SEEPZ worked, Shah ar­gued, be­cause it added a pocket of free­dom, not be­cause any­one picked the right in­dus­try. Its two great win­ners were not on anyone’s list. Firms, he said, will sur­prise us with what they do with free­dom. {089-S08}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s SEEPZ joke: the Allman Brothers Band played there and only Derek Trucks was ex­am­ined, “be­cause we were ex­am­in­ing all the trucks.” {089-J12}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on SEEPZ, diamonds and software

stories.head: Seven years to say hello
body: About 70 per cent of Indians were born after lib­er­al­i­sa­tion, Amit Varma said, so he feels it is his duty to keep retelling sto­ries from be­fore it. {#seventy}
He grew up in a priv­i­leged house­hold; his fa­ther was a civil ser­vant[[x19]]. Yet in the 1980s you waited seven or eight years for a tele­phone from the mo­nop­oly, MTNL[[x20]]. {#phonewait}

Flights cost about what they do now, he re­called, “ex­cept that eight thou­sand ru­pees then was a heck of a lot”. Even an officer’s fam­ily rarely flew, and he still re­mem­bers the ex­cite­ment of his first flight.

~ When the sec­tors opened up in 1991, com­peti­tors flooded in and ev­ery­thing got cheaper. Television chan­nels mul­ti­plied, and no­body needed to watch Doordarshan. The old mo­nop­o­lies sim­ply stopped mat­ter­ing. {089-S06}

quote.text: it’s not that they were shut down, it’s just that they be­came com­pletely ir­rel­e­vant.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah was less con­soled: new pub­lic sec­tor com­pa­nies, he said, are still being cre­ated every year.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the wait for a telephone

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on an airline’s round trip
stories.head: Tata to state and back again
body: Air India began as a pri­vate com­pany owned by the Tatas, Ajay Shah said. The gov­ern­ment ex­pro­pri­ated it and made it a mo­nop­oly.

When the air­line in­dus­try was opened to com­pe­ti­tion, Air India be­came a zom­bie firm[[x21]], kept aloft only by taxpayers’ money. At its peak, Shah be­lieved, it was bleed­ing 35,000 crore ru­pees a year in gov­ern­ment sub­sidy. {#aibleed}
In what he called a great achieve­ment of the BJP gov­ern­ment, it was pri­va­tised and went back to the Tatas.

~ That is a good out­come, Shah said, but it leaves a ques­tion hang­ing: what if Air India had never been na­tion­alised, and the in­dus­try had mul­ti­ple global ri­vals all along? Why does Lufthansa not fly Bombay to Delhi? {089-S07}
stories.why: Privatisation re­cov­ers only part of the loss. The real cost is the decades of com­pe­ti­tion, ser­vice and growth that never hap­pened while the state ran the air­line.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Air India’s long detour

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on how technologies spread
stories.head: Pay by UPI, or pay a fine
body: The hosts’ friend Suyash, Ajay Shah said, had spot­ted some­thing: the gov­ern­ment chose UPI as the tech­nol­ogy and then threw in­come tax law be­hind it. Inspectors can fine any shop that does not ac­cept UPI[[x22]].

Amit Varma ad­mit­ted this was news to him. UPI is out­stand­ing tech­nol­ogy[[x23]], he said, but every shop­keeper should be free to choose how to take pay­ment, be­cause that free­dom is how the best pay­ment sys­tems emerge. {#upi}
Shah of­fered a con­trast. In 1993, he thought, Bill Clinton signed off on re­leas­ing high-resolution GPS data to the whole world. {#clinton} People ran, not walked, to adopt it.
~ Nobody or­dered every phone to carry GPS; phone mak­ers longed for the day it would. India, Shah con­cluded, reaches for force too eas­ily. {089-S05}

quote.text: So it is a very Indian malaise, the low trig­ger point for the use of co­er­cive power

quiz.q: Which two industries made the RBI’s list for cheap foreign borrowing, to Ajay Shah’s amusement?
quiz.a: Nanotechnology and poul­try farms, among nine in­dus­tries al­lowed ex­ter­nal com­mer­cial bor­row­ing.

quiz.q: What, according to Ajay Shah, is the marginal cost of public funds?
quiz.a: About three: each rupee the gov­ern­ment spends costs the econ­omy roughly three.

quiz.q: Which two great industries grew, unplanned, inside the Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone?
quiz.a: Diamond pol­ish­ing and com­puter soft­ware, though the zone was built for ex­port­ing ra­dios.

quiz.q: In the 1980s, how long was the wait for a telephone, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Seven or eight years, be­cause MTNL held a mo­nop­oly on tele­phones.

quiz.q: Whose line did Ajay Shah borrow to urge governments to doubt their technology bets?
quiz.a: Oliver Cromwell’s: in the bow­els of Christ, con­sider it pos­si­ble you may be mis­taken.

quiz.q: In Amit Varma’s riddle, what is the secretary for a leader’s elbows, knees and ankles?
quiz.a: The joint sec­re­tary, the bu­reau­cratic rank the hosts mocked all episode long.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 89. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Oliver Cromwell (After Samuel Cooper, public domain); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Jonathan Rauch (New America, CC BY 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.title: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek names the core error be­hind cen­tral plan­ning and price con­trols: the be­lief that any­one can know enough to run a com­plex so­ci­ety from the top down, when the knowl­edge it needs is spread across ev­ery­one.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah’s conversation with Rahul Ahluwalia
shelf.creator: Rahul Ahluwalia
shelf.why: Amit calls it a lovely chat and the com­pan­ion to this episode’s sub­ject.

shelf.title: Foundation for Economic Development (YouTube channel)
shelf.creator: Rahul Ahluwalia
shelf.why: ‘Rahul’s a great guy... please do check out his chan­nel as well.

shelf.title: Don’t Run a Country Like a Company (Episode 60, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why busi­ness in­tu­itions don’t carry over to pub­lic pol­icy: pol­i­cy­mak­ing is a com­pletely dif­fer­ent and hard-won body of knowl­edge, and for­get­ting that is the trap be­hind many calls for in­dus­trial pol­icy.

shelf.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34) and From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37), Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Episode 56, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A cri­tique of ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic infrastructure’ such as Aadhaar and UPI: state-backed mo­nop­o­lies cre­ated by co­er­cive power, with­out checks and bal­ances, that crowd out com­pet­ing pri­vate sys­tems.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21) and The Journey of Indian Finance (Episode 71), Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Government’s End: Why Washington Stopped Working
shelf.creator: Jonathan Rauch
shelf.why: Rauch’s ac­count of how spe­cial in­ter­ests cap­tured the American state, coin­ing ‘demosclerosis’: in­ter­est groups and reg­u­la­tions mul­ti­ply until they are nearly im­pos­si­ble to re­verse and crowd out other pol­i­cy­mak­ing.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: The Power of Moore’s Laws (Episode 87, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Built around Wright’s Law: pro­duc­tiv­ity rises about 20% with each dou­bling of cu­mu­la­tive out­put, so vol­ume drives down costs and tiny fac­to­ries can’t com­pete, in ser­vices as well as man­u­fac­tur­ing.

shelf.title: The China Model is Broken (Episode 16, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Chinese state con­trol and in­dus­trial pol­icy caused deep prob­lems be­hind the cherry-picked EV and solar suc­cesses: Xi’s cen­tral­i­sa­tion and na­tion­al­ism, cap­i­tal con­trols, real-estate over­build­ing, the exit of for­eign­ers and a failed eq­uity mar­ket.

shelf.title: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Episode 59, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why re­search fund­ing in India is ‘a truly bad space’, and the al­ter­na­tive: an in­dus­try-neutral ap­proach that con­tracts R&D out through grants to uni­ver­si­ties and pri­vate firms rather than hav­ing bu­reau­crats pick sec­tors.

shelf.title: Going Bankrupt in India (Episode 80, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why bank­ruptcy is a healthy, nor­mal part of eco­nomic life, and how the pol­i­tics of India’s bank­ruptcy re­form gave big com­pa­nies out­sized in­flu­ence, left op­er­a­tional cred­i­tors weak and squeezed small manufacturers’ work­ing cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: Life Lessons From Chess in 2024 (Episode 81, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Lessons from chess on why re­newal mat­ters more than mas­tery (ex­perts in nar­row fields stop learn­ing), why young play­ers peak in a fi­nite game, and why a great firm re­cruits from all over the world.

shelf.title: On PLI: Many roads lead to a sound GST
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The writ­ten ver­sion of Ajay’s ar­gu­ment that PLI patches in­di­rect-tax mis­takes that should in­stead be fixed at the root.

shelf.title: India’s supply chain vulnerability with Chinese APIs
shelf.creator: Gautam Bambawale, Vijay Kelkar, Raghunath Mashelkar, Ganesh Natarajan, Ajit Ranade and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay and co-authors on the gen­uine na­tional-security worry about Chinese sup­ply chains, and how to ad­dress it nar­rowly, cleanly and with min­i­mal state in­ter­ven­tion, rather than by dis­tort­ing the whole econ­omy or hand­ing one com­pany at a time a big con­tract.

shelf.title: The Lowest Hanging Fruit On The Coconut Tree: India’s Climate Transition Through The Price System In The Power Sector
shelf.creator: Akhsay Jaitley and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay’s case for a mar­ket-based elec­tric­ity sec­tor that drives India’s cli­mate tran­si­tion through the price sys­tem, rather than the state pick­ing favoured tech­nolo­gies.

shelf.title: Eat a Peach
shelf.creator: The Allman Brothers Band
shelf.why: Amit sin­gles out two tracks, ‘Little Martha’ and ‘Blue Sky’, both fea­tur­ing Duane Allman: ‘Absolutely love his gui­tar­ing, great feel, great vibe, just in­cred­i­ble.’

shelf.title: Layla
shelf.creator: Derek and the Dominos
shelf.why: Ajay in­sists on the orig­i­nal: ‘Be sure to find the right ver­sion of it.

laughs.text: Amit’s ver­sion of the clas­sic $500-bill joke. A Bengali econ­o­mist who be­lieves in ra­tio­nal mar­kets walks past a 500-rupee note, rea­son­ing that if it were real some­one would have picked it up al­ready. Then a Gujarati YouTuber (‘hint hint, wink wink’) spots it and says not ‘money’ but ‘content’, and sets up his selfie stick to film him­self dis­cov­er­ing it. Meanwhile Amit Varma walks up from be­hind and pock­ets it. ‘The story doesn’t end well for ei­ther of our two pro­tag­o­nists.’
After Ajay says he pub­licly de­clared his of­fi­cial oc­cu­pa­tion as YouTuber, Amit: ‘So you are hence­forth not an econ­o­mist. You’re a card car­ry­ing YouTuber.’

On the RBI let­ting poul­try farms bor­row abroad: ‘Amit, you’re not eat­ing enough chicken. Chicken needs cheap credit.’ Amit’s come­back: ‘Picking chick­ens in nan­otech­nol­ogy and re­sult­ing in re­ally tiny chick­ens... we have nano chick­ens.’

Ajay claims YouTube says most view­ers are en­gi­neers. Amit: ‘Wait a minute, what an­a­lyt­ics are you ex­am­in­ing? This is nowhere in the an­a­lyt­ics.’ Ajay: ‘Young males and al­most all young males in India are en­gi­neers.’ Amit: ‘No, many cre­ative women watch our show, I mean partly mainly be­cause of me.’ After Ajay’s rant against en­gi­neers jump­ing to in­dus­trial pol­icy, Amit adds: ‘Gentle read­ers, Ajay Shah is an en­gi­neer.’
Ajay’s trib­ute to the show’s own cam­era crew: ‘If any idiot had a Sony Alpha DSLR, they do not be­come Nomsita.’

Amit on Ajay’s coinage ‘neg­a­tive disability’: ‘At some point some­day, Ajay Shah, peo­ple are gonna come and hit on you and they’ll say things like Ajay, you have so many neg­a­tive dis­abil­i­ties.’ Ajay can’t find a snappy reply, and Amit tells him to bring one next episode.

Amit’s rid­dle: a dear leader ap­points a sec­re­tary for each sys­tem of or­gans, a di­ges­tion sec­re­tary for the stom­ach and a res­pi­ra­tion sec­re­tary for the lungs. What do you call the one in charge of his el­bows, knees and an­kles? Ajay gets it (the joint sec­re­tary, the bu­reau­cratic rank mocked all episode), and Amit says: ‘Well done. I’m so proud of you.’
Amit’s SEEPZ pun: the Allman Brothers Band came to per­form there, ev­ery­one was let in, but one mem­ber was ex­am­ined. Who? Derek Trucks, ‘be­cause we were ex­am­in­ing all the trucks.’

The rec­om­men­da­tions heist. Amit com­plains that every episode he pro­poses a rec­om­men­da­tions chap­ter, the crew ‘break their si­lence and say yes, yes, yes,’ and Ajay says ‘for­get it, next time.’ Then Ajay an­swers Amit’s Duane Allman quiz with ‘Layla’ and de­clares it ‘my rec­om­men­da­tion for today’. Amit: ‘You can­not fuck­ing do this. I had al­ready named the song. This was gonna be my rec­om­men­da­tion.’ Ajay: ‘I prom­ise next episode, I will have five rec­om­men­da­tions.’
Friedrich Hayek’s ‘fatal conceit’: Amit’s name for the hubris of plan­ning a na­tion, and the in­tel­lec­tual back­bone of the episode.
Oliver Cromwell, cited by Ajay against gov­ern­ments sure of their tech­nol­ogy bets: ‘in the bow­els of Christ, con­sider it pos­si­ble you may be mis­taken.’
Milton Friedman’s ma­trix of spend­ing your own or some­one else’s money on your­self or on oth­ers, which Amit uses to show why gov­ern­ment spend­ing is the worst kind.
Ajay’s twist on the open­ing line of Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina: ‘All suc­cess­ful ad­vanced economies look alike. All un­happy, poor coun­tries are un­happy in their own way.’
